question.text: A top-up health insurance plan is beneficial in retirement because:

answer.text: It replaces the need for a base health insurance policy
It provides additional coverage at a lower premium once the base policy limit is exhausted
It covers only outpatient expenses not covered by the base policy
It is available only to individuals below 60 years of age

explanation.text: The Logic: A top-up health insurance plan provides an additional layer of hospitalisation cover that activates once a defined "deductible" threshold has been crossed in a policy year. The deductible can be met by the base health policy's sum insured or by out-of-pocket spend. Because the insurer's risk is limited to claims above this threshold, top-up premiums are materially lower than the cost of buying an equivalent increase in the base policy's sum insured, which makes top-ups particularly attractive for retirees worried about high-cost hospitalisation. The Trap: "Replaces the need for a base health insurance policy" is incorrect — a top-up presumes a deductible that is typically anchored on a base cover. "Covers only outpatient expenses" confuses top-up with OPD or daycare riders; top-ups are predominantly hospitalisation-focused. "Available only below 60" is the opposite of the typical retirement-planning use-case; top-ups are widely available to older lives subject to underwriting. Note: The cited NISM Series XVII Retirement Adviser workbook pages discuss health insurance and ULIP top-ups in different contexts and do not contain a dedicated explanation of health top-up mechanics with deductibles. The framing above is presented as general health-insurance product knowledge, not as a workbook-page citation.
